Tally alternative

Most people should not replace Tally.

If you searched for a Tally alternative, the honest answer is that you probably do not need one. What you need is to stop using Tally for the things it was never built for — stock you can promise, orders in flight, enquiries, follow-ups, receivables somebody has to chase — and keep it doing the statutory books, with a clean export between the two.

What Tally is genuinely excellent at

Tally is fast in a way modern software mostly is not. An accountant who knows it enters a voucher without touching a mouse, and that muscle memory is worth years of training you never had to pay for. It is the reason a two-person accounts team keeps up with a thirty-person business.

It is also the thing your auditor asks for by name. A statutory audit, a bank wanting books before it renews a limit, a query three years later — all of them expect Tally data, and the person answering has done it a hundred times. A one-time licence on a machine in the accounts room, with no dependency on your internet connection, is not a bad deal for that.

So the question is not whether Tally is good. It is whether the work you push through it is accounting work. Most of what a growing business does in a day is not: answering an enquiry, promising a delivery date, deciding whether four hundred bags can be committed to two customers. Tally has no opinion about any of that, because it was never asked to.

The four places a growing business outgrows it

Not four complaints. Four points where the work stops fitting the tool, each with a rough threshold you can check against your own numbers.

  • Stock you can promise. Tally tells you what is on hand. It has no concept of what is already committed to an open order, so the figure on the screen and the figure you can safely quote against are different, and the difference lives in somebody's head. This starts costing money at around two locations or thirty to forty orders a month, whichever arrives first.
  • Everything before the invoice. An enquiry, a quote, a follow-up, a reason a deal was lost — none of them are transactions yet, so none of them exist in Tally. The first time the business records a customer properly is the day it invoices them.
  • One room, one machine. Tally is built around a computer in the accounts department. Add a second godown or four salespeople who are never at a desk and you are either synchronising licences or photographing screens onto WhatsApp. In practice it is the second one.
  • Nothing checks the credit you are about to claim. Tally records the tax on a purchase bill. It does not know whether your supplier actually filed that invoice, which is the only thing that decides whether the credit is yours. On a 40 lakh monthly purchase run at 18 percent, roughly 7 lakh a month rides on other people's filing discipline, and the first symptom of trouble is a notice.

Who keeps what after the move

The split we implement on almost every project. Nobody gives up the books, and the auditor's answer to every question stays where it has always been.

The workRuns in OrdenceStays in Tally
Enquiries, quotes, follow-upsAll of itNothing. It was never there
Orders, stock, dispatchAvailability net of commitmentsNothing
Sales invoices and credit notesRaised here, GST computed hereReceived as vouchers
Purchase bills and the ITC registerRecorded, matched to GSTR-2BReceived as vouchers
Receivables and ageingChased here, computed onceBalances agree
Ledgers, trial balance, balance sheetNot hereBook of record
Returns and filingPrepared, never submittedYour CA files

What moving actually costs, in time and disruption

Not the licence and not the subscription. The cost is attention from one person who knows how the work really happens — a few hours a week during the build, closer to a day a week during the pilot. If that person does not exist, no amount of software design rescues the project, and it is better to find that out now than in week nine.

The second cost is an argument you have been postponing. Somewhere in your data are four spellings of one customer, an opening balance nobody can tie to a trial balance, and two people who each believe their own stock figure. Migration forces a decision about which record wins. That is a business judgement, and the week it takes is a week you would have spent later under worse conditions.

The third is a fortnight where two systems disagree while people learn. We shorten it by reconciling the migration against a number you already trust — the receivables total, the closing stock value — rather than against itself. For a standard scope the whole thing is weeks. Heavy history or several teams pushes it toward a staged quarter, written on the scope with the price.

When to stay exactly where you are

Every line here is a reason not to buy from us. Better read on a Tuesday afternoon than heard on the fourth call.

  • Under ten people, one location, under about thirty orders a month. You do not have a systems problem yet. You have a busy month.
  • Reconciling your sheets against your books takes under half a day a month. The pain has to be recurring and measurable before a migration pays for itself.
  • Your peak season starts within six weeks. Go live after it. A pilot during the busiest fortnight of your year is how people revert and never come back.
  • What you actually need is e-invoicing. We generate no IRNs and have no IRP connection, so if that is the gap, a Tally connector solves it and we do not.
  • Nobody on your side can be the named owner. Not a name on a slide, a person with hours. Without them this becomes the vendor's project, and the vendor's project fails.

Questions people actually ask

So Ordence is not a Tally replacement?

Correct, and by design rather than omission. Building the second-best answer to a question the auditor is not asking would be a poor use of a small team. Some customers move the books across once operations are stable. Most do not, and are right not to.

What should we test on the demo call?

Three things. Export the same batch twice and check Tally updates the voucher rather than creating a second one. Break a ledger mapping on purpose and see whether it is visible before the export or silently drops those transactions. And ask how the file actually reaches Tally, because Tally answers on your office network and a cloud server cannot reach it.

Our accountant is against this.

Get them on the second call, not the tenth. The objection is almost always a specific fear that Tally is about to be taken away, and it is not. If they still object after seeing the re-runnable voucher export and the GSTR-2B reconciliation, that objection is information worth having.

Send us one month of your Tally data.

Before you sign anything. We will tell you in writing what imports cleanly, what does not, and whether the honest answer is to stay put another year.
